title: Chapter 2.  Geography — Rivers, Lakes, Climate & the Cold Desert

blocks.content: Ladakh's defining ecological character is that of a 'cold desert' - extremely low precipitation combined with extreme cold - a combination found in very few other parts of India, making this chapter rich in distinctive, frequently tested climatic and hydrological facts.
The Indus River & Ladakh's River Systems

The Indus River is Ladakh's defining river, flowing through the region for a substantial stretch and forming the historic and settlement core of Ladakhi civilisation, with Leh and most major towns and monasteries situated along or near its course.

The Zanskar River, a major tributary of the Indus, drains the rugged Zanskar valley in southern Ladakh before joining the Indus near Nimmu - a confluence point ('Sangam') popular for river-rafting tourism and notable for the visible colour contrast between the two rivers' waters.
The Shyok River, another major tributary, flows through the Nubra valley region in northern Ladakh, joining the Indus further downstream in Pakistan-administered territory.
The Suru River drains the Kargil area in western Ladakh, eventually joining the Indus system as well, and is significant for Kargil district's agriculture and settlement pattern.

cells: Flows through central Ladakh via Leh district
Defining river of Ladakhi civilisation; Ladakh's stretch is within India's non-consumptive-use rights under the Indus Waters Treaty
Drains the Zanskar valley, joins Indus at Nimmu ('Sangam')
Major tributary; associated with the Nubra Valley's distinctive sand-dune, high-altitude-desert landscape
Key river for Kargil district's agriculture and settlement
Eastern Ladakh, extending across the LAC into China

A long, narrow endorheic (landlocked, saline) lake famous for its colour-changing waters; strategically significant given its cross-LAC extent; a major tourism draw following its feature in popular Indian cinema
A high-altitude freshwater/brackish lake, part of the Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary and a Ramsar-designated wetland; important habitat for the black-necked crane and other high-altitude bird species
A smaller saline lake, also within the Changthang high-altitude ecosystem, historically associated with local salt extraction

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Pangong Tso extends across the LAC into Chinese-controlled territory (roughly two-thirds of the lake lies on the Chinese side) - a frequently tested geography-cum-strategic fact, given the lake's periodic prominence in India-China border tension reporting.

Ladakh's climate is classified as a high-altitude cold desert, characterised by extremely low annual precipitation (much of the region receives less than 100 mm of precipitation annually, comparable to hot desert regions, but in the form of light snow rather than rain) combined with extreme temperature swings - very cold winters (temperatures regularly falling below -20C to -30C in Leh and lower in more remote areas) and relatively mild, intensely sunny summers.

This aridity arises directly from Ladakh's position in the rain-shadow of the Great Himalaya/Zanskar ranges (Chapter 1), which block the bulk of the monsoon's moisture before it can reach the Trans-Himalayan zone.

Because of this extreme aridity, Ladakhi agriculture and settlement have historically depended entirely on glacier/snowmelt-fed irrigation channels rather than rainfall, a traditional water-management system that remains central to the region's rural economy and has inspired modern innovations such as artificial glaciers/'ice stupas' (see Chapter 11).

★ EXAM POINT: 'Cold desert' is THE defining climatic term for Ladakh - remember it combines desert-level ARIDITY (rain-shadow effect) with extreme COLD (high altitude), distinguishing it clearly from both the hot deserts of Rajasthan and the wetter, temperate Kashmir Valley just across the Zanskar/Great Himalaya divide.

items: The Changthang Plateau, in south-eastern Ladakh, is the Indian portion of the wider Tibetan Changtang plateau, a high-altitude (average elevation above 4,300 m) rangeland extending into Tibet, historically home to the semi-nomadic Changpa pastoral community (Chapter 9).

Changthang is ecologically significant as the source of Pashmina wool (from the Changra goat breed reared by Changpa herders), a major economic link to the Kashmir Valley's shawl-weaving industry, and as a critical habitat zone protected under the Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary (Chapter 11).
Indus = Ladakh's defining river; Zanskar, Shyok and Suru are its major tributaries.
Pangong Tso: endorheic saline lake, ~2/3 extends into Chinese-controlled territory across the LAC.
Tso Moriri: Ramsar wetland, key black-necked crane habitat, Changthang plateau.
Ladakh's climate = high-altitude 'cold desert' - extreme aridity (rain-shadow) + extreme cold; agriculture depends on glacier/snowmelt irrigation, not rainfall.
Changthang Plateau: source of Pashmina wool (Changra goats, reared by semi-nomadic Changpa herders).
